summary: Delay-Tolerant Networking covers networks hit by long delays or frequent link disruptions. This informational document describes a management architecture suited to that setting, supporting asynchronous transport and autonomous local control.

plainLanguage.summary: Imagine running a probe far out in space where messages take ages. This describes how to look after such a network when you cannot talk to it instantly.

subtitle: Managing networks with long delays, frequent link disruptions, and remote operations.

tldr.problem: Traditional network management assumes timely request-response exchanges and permanent connections. Challenged networks (with long delays, frequent disruptions, or unidirectional links) cannot guarantee round-trip exchanges, making pull-based management and real-time control impossible.
tldr.mechanism: DTNMA defines a logical architecture with DTNMA Agents (DAs) on managed devices that operate autonomously using preconfigured policies, and DTNMA Managers (DMs) on managing devices that configure policies and collect reports asynchronously. Management uses push-based information flows and rule-based local autonomy rather than request-response.
tldr.outcome: Devices can manage themselves during extended periods of disconnection. DMs configure policy rules once during connectivity, and DAs execute those rules locally. Reports are queued and transmitted when links become available. This supports deep-space missions, satellite networks, ocean buoys, and other challenged environments.

facts.label: Transport agnostic
facts.value: Does not require IP, TCP, DNS, or CAs

facts.label: Data flow
facts.value: Push-based (DAs push reports), not pull-based (no manager queries)

facts.label: Management relationship
facts.value: Many-to-many (multiple DMs can manage one DA)

today: RFC 9675 is an Informational RFC documenting a logical management architecture suitable for challenged networks. The DTNMA is being adopted by space agencies and researchers working with delay-tolerant systems, though no standardized protocol fully implements it yet. The architecture provides guidance for designing management protocols for satellite, deep-space, ocean, and other challenged environments.

sections.title: Management in Challenged Networks
sections.content:
Challenged networks have properties that prevent timely end-to-end communication: long signal propagation delays (seconds to hours), frequent link disruptions, lack of end-to-end IP connectivity, unidirectional links, or asymmetric link capacities. Examples include deep space communications, satellite networks, underwater systems, and energy-harvesting sensor networks.

The DTN (Delay-Tolerant Networking) architecture was designed for these environments. Just as DTN required new transport protocols (like the Bundle Protocol), network management in such environments requires a new approach. Traditional management protocols like SNMP, NETCONF, and RESTCONF rely on timely round-trip exchanges and stateful connections—assumptions that do not hold in challenged networks.

DTNMA provides a logical management architecture suitable for challenged networks. It emphasizes asynchronous transport (no round-trip requirements), autonomous local control (devices self-manage when disconnected), and small footprint (suitable for resource-constrained devices). The architecture is agnostic to the underlying transport protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: When you manage a device very far away and messages take a long time, you cannot ask 'Are you okay?' and wait for an answer. Instead, you send instructions once, and the device figures things out on its own.

sections.title: Key Concepts: Agents and Managers
sections.content:
DTNMA defines two primary roles:

DTNMA Agent (DA): Software running on a managed device that monitors local applications, controls their behavior through predefined rules, generates data reports, and handles local autonomy. A DA performs three major functions: (1) Monitoring and Control using an autonomy engine that evaluates rules and issues commands to local applications, (2) Data Fusion that synthesizes new data values from raw application state (reducing the volume of data to transmit), and (3) Administration including authorization, access control, and manager mappings.

DTNMA Manager (DM): Software running on a managing device that encodes management policies, sends them to agents, and receives and analyzes reports. A DM translates policy directives from managing applications into standardized autonomy rules. The DM does not expect real-time responses; it operates in an 'open-loop' mode where commands are sent without waiting for confirmation.

The critical difference from traditional management is that management is two-tiered. Tier 2 involves a DM configuring a DA with policies. Tier 1 is how those policies are transported (NETCONF, RESTCONF, or custom mechanisms). This separation allows DAs to manage themselves between connectivity windows.
sections.plainLanguage: An Agent is like a local manager on the device that knows what to do. A Manager is like a remote boss who sends instructions. The boss sends one big instruction set, then the local manager handles everything until the boss calls again.

sections.title: Autonomous Operation with Rules
sections.content:
The heart of DTNMA is a rule-based autonomy model where each rule is a stimulus-response pair: IF condition THEN action. The DA's autonomy engine continuously evaluates rule conditions against the device's current state and executes responses when conditions are met.

Stimuli are predicate logic expressions that examine device state. A stimulus might be 'temperature > 80 degrees' or 'no reports sent in 1 hour'. Responses are Controls (parameterized procedures on the device) or rule database updates. When a stimulus is detected, the DA issues Controls to applications or generates reports to managers.

Pre-shared definitions are critical because devices cannot negotiate in real-time. DMs and DAs agree on three types of definitions before deployment: (1) the autonomy model (which rule structures are allowed), (2) application data models (what data each application exposes and what controls it accepts), and (3) runtime datastores (custom data synchronized between DAs and DMs during connectivity).
sections.plainLanguage: Rules are like instructions: 'If the battery is low, turn off the radio and save power. If we have not heard from the boss in 3 days, try the backup communication plan.' The device follows these rules without asking for permission each time.

sections.title: Design Principles for Challenged Networks
sections.content:
DTNMA is built on seven desirable design properties that distinguish it from traditional management architectures:

Dynamic Architectures: No dependency on specific physical topologies, transports, or infrastructure. The architecture does not require IP, TCP, DNS, or Certificate Authorities to be present.

Hierarchically Modeled Information: Data models define contracts between DAs and DMs. Cohesive, modular models can be combined hierarchically to describe complex management scenarios.

Adaptive Push of Information: DAs push data to DMs based on their local state, not in response to manager queries. Avoid pull mechanisms that require timely round-trip exchanges.

Efficient Data Encoding: Messages should be compressible and compact. Smaller messages require shorter transmission windows and incur less retransmission cost.

Universal, Unique Data Identification: Data elements are identified by universal identifiers that do not change over time or across implementations, avoiding reliance on relative indexing.

Runtime Data Definitions: New data elements can be added to the system at runtime, allowing custom data fusion or specialized reporting without changing baseline definitions.

Autonomous Operation: Devices operate deterministically and autonomously during disconnection. Preconfigured behaviors are triggered by local stimuli, with optional authorization and accounting from local or remote sources.
sections.plainLanguage: The architecture is flexible (works in any environment), organized (uses clear definitions), pushes information (do not wait for questions), is small (saves bandwidth), has clear names (no confusion), allows custom additions (new rules for new situations), and works alone (when disconnected).

sections.title: The DTNMA Reference Model
sections.content:
The reference model identifies four functional elements:

Managed Applications and Services reside on the managed device. These are the software entities (routing protocols, sensors, propulsion systems) that the DA monitors and controls. The DA must have a data model describing each application's state variables and control procedures.

DTNMA Agent (DA) is responsible for monitoring, controlling, and reporting on managed applications. The DA's autonomy engine evaluates rules periodically or when triggered by events. Reports are generated and queued for transmission, independent of manager connectivity.

Managing Applications and Services reside on the managing device and represent operators or automated management systems. They request policies (like 'send a report every 60 seconds') but do not expect immediate responses.

DTNMA Manager (DM) translates managing application policies into DTNMA autonomy rules and sends them to DAs. It also collects and analyzes reports from DAs to understand system state.

Pre-Shared Definitions (autonomy model, application data models, runtime datastores) are synchronized between DMs and DAs during connectivity, allowing them to communicate unambiguously even during extended disconnections.
sections.plainLanguage: The setup has four parts: applications that need managing, local managers (agents) that oversee them, remote managers that send policies, and a shared handbook both sides agree on.

sections.title: DTNMA Services and Use Cases
sections.content:
DTNMA provides five core services:

Local Monitoring and Control: DAs monitor application state at regular intervals and autonomously control applications based on preconfigured rules. Unlike traditional management, control happens locally without waiting for manager input.

Local Data Fusion: DAs synthesize new data from existing state (averaging counters, computing derived values). Fusion occurs on the managed device, reducing transmitted data volume and enabling local decision-making.

Remote Configuration: DMs update DA configurations via policy rules. Configuration is state-dependent (apply different rules based on current conditions) rather than a simple datastore replacement.

Remote Reporting: DAs produce and queue reports independently of manager connectivity. Reports are timestamped, tagged with the stimulus that triggered them, and transmitted when links become available, possibly arriving out of order.

Authorization: Both DAs and DMs enforce access control. A DM may only configure certain applications, and a DA may only report to authorized managers. Multiple managers can coexist on a network, each with different permissions.

Use cases include: serialized management (one DM configuring multiple DAs), intermittent connectivity (DAs queue reports during outages), open-loop reporting (many-to-one mapping between policies and reports), multiple administrative domains (different managers control different parts of a device), and cascading management (a device acts as both DA and DM).
sections.plainLanguage: DTNMA lets devices watch themselves, combine data to send less, accept new instructions from distant managers, report back whenever they get a chance, and follow access rules. It supports complex scenarios like multiple managers or relay devices.
